utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the accused are all here, and the Defence teams are all here. Do you feel any heavier now, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Prosecution is here. If there are problems with interpretation at any time, please let us know. As you may have noticed or you would have surely have noticed, we are sitting without Judge Prost today, and that will remain to be so the rest of this week, and we will be sitting in terms of Rule 15 bis, first paragraph, (A). She will be with us again next week, or this coming week. Thank you. Now, this first witness that we have, we're talking of witness number 66; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We are actually confirming orally now the protective measures that we had originally put in place for this witness, and for the purpose of his testimony, we are granting pseudonym, face distortion, and voice distortion. The other thing we wanted to raise with you orally, and let's dispose of it today, because I don't like playing ping-pong during the sittings, is the following: Witness -- next witness, the following one, then, witness number 98. Now, in your motion, in a request you have actually sought facial distortion and pseudonym, while in the body of the motion itself, there is an indication that you are seeking also voice distortion. We authorised our staff to try and elucidate this and only to find out that at one point it seems the witness wanted only voice -- only facial distortion and pseudonym and that very soon after he reiterated his first request, namely, one which was inclusive also of voice distortion. So I want to know exactly now, please, what you're seeking so that I can then turn to the Defence to see if they have any objection to including also voice distortion, although it is not so requested in your motion. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. You're entirely correct. We, inadvertently, in the actual body of the request, did not seek the voice distortion although we mentioned it in the introduction. The witness at issue has confirmed as recently as yesterday afternoon that he does wish the voice distortion means as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's leave it at that. You have already indicated that you don't have any objection to facial and -- distortion and pseudonym. I take it that you do not object for -- to including also voice distortion? I don't know who wants to taking the responsibility. Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, we don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't. Okay. So we're handing down an oral decision now which will probably be followed by a written decision. It's all prepared. And the protective measures sought which will be granted are precisely the ones I mention earlier, the three of them in other words. And that applies to Witness 98, who will be Prosecution Witness 107. This one who is going to start giving evidence now will be Witness PW-106. Thank you. Other preliminaries? Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Last night at 1.00 in the morning we received the proofing notes for the witness who is about to testify today. He is a protected witness, and we have received very little information about him. So these proofing notes that were received in the course of the night includes information we never heard about. We couldn't think that the witness was about to testify on these topics. So I don't know how the Prosecutor can imagine that the Defence are able to properly prepare their cross-examinations if they receive proofing notes with totally new information only three or four hours before the hearing begins, before the witness begins to testify. I do not want to ask for the report as to the testimony of this witness. I don't know how long the examination-in-chief will be, but I will request for the cross-examination not to start today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who is responding to this? Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. The proofing notes did go out at 1.00 this morning. I was probably as less happy about that as anybody was receiving them at that hour because that's when I completed it, having proofed this witness and the next witness back to back given their travel schedules. The information concerning the incident itself that was added in the proofing notes is relatively minor. The Defence has had the unredacted, full information report of this witness regarding that incident for some time now. There is additional information concerning the situation in the enclave in 1992, 1993, and into 1995, which is new. I believe that there will be adequate opportunity to cross-examine this witness based on the incident that is described in great detail in the information report and which was not enhanced, I would submit, to any substantial degree in the proofing notes. So I don't believe there's -- there's a compelling reason to completely delay the cross-examination. I believe substantive cross-examination could commence today, and if the Defence needs more time to analyse the proofing notes during the various breaks, perhaps, there can be a reassessment towards the middle or the end of the day in that regard. It may -- it may be a mooted issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I briefly respond --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- as to the incident mentioned by Mr. Thayer. I think this is the major part of the witness's testimony. We knew what he was about to speak but that part did not have anything to do especially with my client. The part that has been added to the proofing notes does concern my client. So this is something for which I, in particular, was not prepared. I did not intend to cross-examine him and now I can see that there's a whole part that's been added which is the major part of the proofing notes we received today, and without being prepared at all, I'm expected to cross-examine the witness. I cannot do that. Plus we have a time period of 24 hours prior to the cross-examination in which we have to have documents put into the e-court system. How could I prepare myself if I receive proofing notes at 1.00 in the morning when the witness is about to arrive at 9.00?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We'd just like to associate ourselves with those comments, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Let me before consulting my two colleagues just point out something. According to the information that we have, the Prosecution requires about two and a half hours for the direct. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And I think I may actually be able to do it in about two hours. The -- and if I just may put in a little bit of context the reason for some of the new information. Based on our continual review of our witness list and our continued wish to try to streamline our witness list, we believe that we may be actually able to eliminate certain witnesses by eliciting related information through other witnesses. This is such a witness. He was new to us. We first interviewed him in May of 2006. The conditions within the Srebrenica enclave, the humanitarian conditions and so forth, are a part of the indictment. This is information that has been repeatedly elicited through -- through other witnesses, and it was new information that we developed through this witness. That is ultimately the reason why we are seeking to elicit this new information, and we're hoping actually to save time in the long run by doing it this way. I understand Madam Fauveau's concerns, but again, it's not entirely new information in the sense that it's information that's unfamiliar in its nature to the Defence. It's basically the same type of information that this Trial Chamber's heard through other Srebrenica inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So let me try to recapitulate and think aloud a little bit. The totality of the Defence teams prior to receiving the proofing notes had indicated a total of three and a half hours for all the cross-examinations put together. That included 30 minutes each from the Defence teams of Generals Miletic and Gvero. Eliminating for the time being cross-examination by these two teams for today, we are still talking of two hours to two and half hours Prosecution and two and a half hours maximum the rest of the Defence teams that do not have any objection with cross-examining the witness today. Basically, that means that today -- today's sitting will not be sufficient in itself to cover both the direct and the rest of the cross-examinations, as I explain. So we are definitely going into tomorrow in any case. Going into tomorrow, I think the problem is eliminated both for you, Madam Fauveau, and for Mr. Krgovic or Mr. Josse, and I think we can work on that assumption and try to head towards that direction. Judge Kwon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And in any case, if it is necessary just to make sure to accommodate you if -- if it is necessary we will get in the next witness to start the -- the direct and then you will have the -- in the meantime, I mean, I appreciate that this has not been blown up into an incident, and in future, let's try to, as much as possible, avoid having these incidents recurring. I know sometimes they have to recur but they are about to create problems. So any further -- but you can put your mind at rest. You will not be cross-examining this witness today, either of you. Any further preliminaries? None. Curtains down, please. And we are going to bring in the next witness, who is a protected witness. The curtains will be down only until he walks in so that his face is not seen, but then the transmission of the proceedings will be in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. You are going to be giving evidence in trial, which is the Srebrenica 2 trial. You've been summoned here to testify by the Prosecution. Our rules require that before you start giving evidence you make a solemn declaration to the effect that in the course of your testimony you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is going to be handed to you now. Please read it out in a way that we can hear you, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Please make yourself comfortable. Take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you start giving evidence, I wish to confirm to you that we have granted you three protective measures, the use of a pseudonym. In other words, we'll hide your name. You will be given a number. You will be known here as PW, Prosecution Witness 106, and you will testify with both facial and voice distortion. I take it these have been explained to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And they are to your satisfaction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So, Mr. Thayer will be examining you in chief. That will take most of today, and then we will move on to the various cross-examinations, but we will not finish with you today. In other words, you will be here again tomorrow for further cross-examination. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Usual reminder. Since the witness is testifying with voice distortion, just make sure that at any time when he is saying something, testifying or whatever, no microphones are on except his. All right? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, Madam Usher is about to hand you a document. I would ask that you read it to yourself and ask if you can confirm that your name is printed under the number PW-106.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That will remain under seal, of course, and we'll give it a number later.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Witness, I would just ask you to move a little bit closer to the microphone and just ask you, before answering a question, whether it's from myself, my learned colleagues on the Defence or the Trial Chamber, just to wait until you've heard the entire question translated and pause before you give your answer. And, Witness, if you need a break at any time, please just let us know. Okay?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we may go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. Thayer. Let's do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Witness, when you arrived in Srebrenica in what area of the town did you at first live?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: At first I lived in -- on an elevation above Srebrenica in a village the name of which was Seoce.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you tell the Trial Chamber if that is anywhere near the area of Kazan or Kazani.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: This is not far from Kazan at an elevation above Kazan itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: When you arrived in Srebrenica, were there other refugees in the town already?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Where were they from, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: They were from Vlasenica, Zvornik, Bratunac, and some other neighbouring municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Could you describe for the Trial Chamber the living conditions that you encountered in Srebrenica at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: Disastrous, both in humanitarian sense as well as in security sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Could you provide some examples, please, of each of those senses that you've just described.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: For example, it was winter. It was March, 1993. There was a lot of snow. It was cold. There was a lack of clothes and footwear, and the biggest problem was a major lack of food. So people started dying of starvation. Already in March, 1993, the situation was terrible, and that was before it fell into the Serb hands for the first -- first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Witness, you referred to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment. Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I believe we have some problem with interpretation, because here in transcript it says it was before it fell to the Serb hands for the first time. It's page 14, line 4 and 5. The witness says as it almost fell into Serb hands, because there is no proof that in 1993 Srebrenica fell into Serb hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 1992, yes, but not 1993. You are a hundred per cent right. Yes. I think we need to clear this -- I mean, it's common knowledge that Srebrenica was taken by the Serbs in 1992, and then it was again retaken by the Muslims in the same year, 1992, in May. We're talking of May. And now we're talking of March 1993. I don't think I've heard anywhere that in March, 1993, the Serbs walked into Srebrenica and took it over. So you need to address this.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Witness, did you understand the --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- Trial Chamber's statement, and in your experience, was that an accurate description of the events of 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because I want to make sure that Mr. Lazarevic is happy with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, I just hope that witness understood what Your Honour said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is why I'm saying it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll just go ahead and ask the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you can easily do that. The witness said -- I'll address you myself. According to the transcript, I don't know actually what you said in your own language, but what we were told you said in English is the following: "Already in March, 1993, the situation was terrible, and that was before it fell into the Serb hands for the first time." What did you mean by that? Because in March, 1993, or in April, 1993, Srebrenica did not fall into the hands of the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, but it was on the verge of falling into Serb hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that explains it, and now it exactly tallies with what Mr. Lazarevic had pointed out. Thank you. You may proceed with your line of questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Witness, you describe the situation as being disastrous also from a security sense. Could you please just briefly describe what you meant by that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: From the very centre of town towards the closest hills, you could see Serb soldiers deployed there. However, in that chaos, the French general, Morillon, would appear and he would try to calm the situation down, and soon after that Srebrenica was proclaimed a safe haven by the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Prior to General Morillon's arrival, Witness, had the Serb forces actually been attacking the enclave itself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: Yes. The villages around Srebrenica came under their attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Witness, were you personally present when General Morillon arrived in March of 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: Yes, I was present. He was at the post office, and I was next to the post office with the crowd that looked to Morillon for help.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what, if anything, did you do at that time, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: At that time we were expecting further information as to how to proceed, whether the population would be evacuated or whether the world would at that point in time help Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you personally participate in any action with respect to General Morillon while he was in Srebrenica at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: At some point after General Morillon's visit, did humanitarian aid begin to arrive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: Not immediately. After a certain time it did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how did the food arrive, sir, or the humanitarian aid arrive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: First of all, there were air drops, and after that, the first UNHCR convoys reached us.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: During this period of time, was there shelling from the Serb forces still?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: As Morillon was leaving, a major massacre took place in the playground next to the school in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you describe any personal knowledge you have about that incident, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: After the incident, I went by that place, and I could observe a host of massacred bodies and half-dead people lying there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Had you been at that location prior to this incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: Of course I was at the gathering where a number of young people gathered in order to celebrate the proclamation of the safe haven. We wanted to celebrate. Fortunately enough, I had left the place of crime some five minutes before the actual crime took place, so I managed to avoid -- avoid the fate of my other friends and colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Witness, did your mother and sister stay in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: No. They left with the convoys that brought food. As they were leaving empty, people would get on those lorries and would go to the free territory. Those were UNHCR convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we may go into private session for just one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. Thayer. Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, have you left the incident of the alleged massacre in the playground.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Something tells me I haven't, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'd like to hear what the witness personally actually knew at the time. It was not clear on the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Witness, did you understand His Honour's question?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: No, not really.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Very well. Would you please provide, Witness, some more detail about the actual event that occurred at that playground, what you were doing; what you saw; what the cause, as you understood it, of this event was; and what, if anything, you did following this incident.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: The Serbs at the observation points must have noticed the group of people that had gathered there. And I don't know what happened. Some five or ten minutes later, I passed by that place and I could see dismembered human bodies, legs and arms, and according to some unofficial information, some 60 people got killed and some 60 or maybe even more than that were wounded, seriously or slightly wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: What was your understanding of the cause of this destruction, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: The cause was to destroy as many people, as many civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Witness, the question is: What killed those people?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The shells that fell --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: If it please the Court, I let this go on. These questions are just purely speculative in nature. The witness has testified he went by afterwards and noticed some bodies, but now to ask him what caused this, it's just purely speculative and I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know what his answers going to be and then we'll decide if it's speculative or not. If it is speculative, of course, as if it has not been stated, but if it is not speculative, it will remain there. And again -- go ahead Mr. Thayer. Repeat your question and let him answer it and then we'll see afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'll rephrase it slightly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, you indicated that you past the playground and then returned. Was there something that caused you to return to the playground?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: I returned because I had heard shells falling at that place. After that, everything came to a -- a standstill, and I realised that there must have been a tragedy there having been aware of the fact how many people had remained in that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you accompany any of the wounded to the hospital, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't have any objection to the line of questioning, but I have an objection to the relevance of this line of questioning. This alleged incident took place in 1993, which is beyond the scope of the indictment. I don't see the point and the relevance of this line of questioning that goes beyond the scope of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It is I that asked Mr. Thayer to proceed. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will move on. I was just trying to provide that detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We will now move to 1995, Witness. Were you still living in Srebrenica at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And with whom were you living?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: With my father.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And at some point in 1995, did you notice a change in how often humanitarian aid convoys were arriving in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: Of course I noticed a change. At the beginning of 1995, the humanitarian situation got worse. All of a sudden, lots of people were forced to start begging for food.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how else did people try to find food?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: In addition to begging, many were forced to go to Zepa crossing a very dangerous road. There was a lot more registered refugees and a lot more food there, and that's why the people of Srebrenica went there to find food. And as they did that, some of them hit the minefields and got killed, and all that because they went in search for food.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: How dependent were you, Witness, personally, on the humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: A hundred per cent. I depended on that a hundred per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And again now briefly, Witness, can you just describe the general conditions, living conditions, in Srebrenica in 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: There were increasingly fewer convoys with humanitarian aid. There was not enough things to maintain hygiene. Wounded started arriving with feet and legs missing. People did not feel safe there. They could sense that there would be some chaos.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in 1995, sir, did -- were you working? Did you have a job?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We need to redact this. And if you are proceeding with this, I think we need to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes. There will be some further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Witness, was there enough money to pay you for your work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: No. I did not receive any money for my work. I volunteered. It was part of the humanitarian aspect of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, prior to 1995, in connection with your work, without getting into specifics, did you see or learn about civilians who had been injured by shelling?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: Yes, there were such cases. I saw such civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: How about civilians injured by sniping?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: There were such individual cases as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And at some point in 1995, Witness, did you observe a change in the number of wounded civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: Well, during the time surrounding the very fall of Srebrenica, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: When you refer to the very fall of Srebrenica, approximately what time period are you talking about, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: I'm referring to a period of a month or so prior to the fall.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to speak with some of those civilians about how they had been wounded during that one- or two-month period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: Yes. They would be brought to the hospital and were nursed by us. And as I've already told you, as they were searching for food and as they were crossing the territory to go to Zepa, they would either hit an ambush or a minefield. The others were wounded as they were collecting fuel, wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you have an occasion to speak with any civilians who had been injured by shells or sniping during this period of time two months prior to the fall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: No, personally, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Your Honour, but this is a speculative question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's answered anyway now. So each time you have -- let's leave it, because the way he has answered it doesn't do any damage in any case. So, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Through your work, sir, without getting into specifics about it, did you receive any information about how civilians had been injured other than stepping on mines?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: [French on English channel]. They were working in the fields not far from the Serb lines, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And -- and what happened to those -- [French on English channel].

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: [French on English channel].

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'm receiving French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And we are receiving French too. So we need to go through this again.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll just repeat my question from page 24, line 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Witness, through your work, without getting into the specifics of what your work was, did you receive information about how civilians had been injured other than by stepping on mines?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: They were also wounded in ambushes. And many of them towards the end felt that Srebrenica was unstable terrain and they were trying to get through to the free territory, and they were then coming up against Serb ambushes and barriers.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Witness, during the entire time you were in Srebrenica, were there adequate medical supplies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: No. As for the medical supplies and other necessary materials, there was a shortage of the most essential supplies as well as a shortage of medical staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to turn your attention now to early July, 1995. Would you tell the Trial Chamber where you were when the VRS actually attacked the enclave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: At that point I was at my workplace.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we'll need to go into private session for a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then we will do that. Let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we are in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Witness, when you left your place of employment, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: I went in the direction of Kazani.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what, if anything, did you encounter there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: There was a very large group of people that were directed to that terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Was there any particular landmark in that area around which people were gathering or near which people were gathering?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: At the exit of Srebrenica, near Kazani, it was a kind of valley. There were radio -- ham radio operators there who managed to send out the last report and to ask for help, since Srebrenica was already in Serb hands. However, they received information to wait and that NATO alliance planes would react and that Srebrenica -- that the people should not leave Srebrenica yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Would you describe for the Trial Chamber, Witness, what the scene was like when you left your place of business and moved towards this location. What did you see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: I saw a larger group of prominent people, and this was via these ham radio operators who were sending out reports and asking for help.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you see whether Srebrenica civilians were heading in any particular direction or directions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because I think the previous answer, at least as it appears in the transcript, elicits some kind of clarification. The question was: "Would you describe for the Trial Chamber what the scene was like when you left your place of business and moved towards this location. What did you see?" So you are asking of the witness his visual perception. And his answer was: "I saw a large group of prominent people." So far so good. I mean it would only elicit "Now, where exactly did you see this large group of prominent people?" It's the next part that is confusing. "And this was via these ham radio operators who were sending out reports and asking for help." That confuses a little bit the issue because what you're asking of him is what he saw and now he jumps in and puts these ham radio operators. So let's deal with that first before you move to your next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Witness, again, what exactly did you see as you left your place of business and were moving towards this area that you described before? What did you see yourself? Can you describe the scene for the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: Yes. The question is clearer to me now. When I left my place of business, at the gas station where a team of the DutchBat was stationed, I saw a vast mass of civilians, the civilian population, and they were going in the direction of Potocari.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, I hate to interrupt and intervene like this, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Do deal with it --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because now we hear nothing about these ham radio operators.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And also, previously, he said, "I saw a larger group of prominent people." And I would have imagined or expected him to explain exactly what he meant by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, you referred in your answer a couple of questions ago to a large group of prominent people and you also referred to some ham radio operators. Would you please clarify those statements for the Trial Chamber, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: Yes. These were people such as the hospital director, the ham radio operators, and people from the municipal institutions who were making a plan and programme in which direction and how to move out, whether to wait for the aviation or to continue on our path of uncertainty towards the free territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I still don't understand. Where did you see this group of prominent people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right at the exit of Srebrenica, at the Kazani location where the rest of the column and the people joined them and then continued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You also mentioned previously a bus loaded with persons that were going into the direction of Potocari. Were these prominent people -- were these prominent people on that bus or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't mention a bus at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the meantime, I think I can hopefully help clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, you referred to civilians heading towards Potocari. From what you saw, how were they heading towards Potocari, by what means?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: On foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And that group of people, sir, did they include men, women, and children, or was it predominantly one sort or the other of people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: The group that I was in?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'm referring to the group that you saw heading towards Potocari, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: Yes, it was a mixed group: Civilians, able-bodied people, women, the elderly.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you also referred to a group that you joined, and I believe you referred to it at one time as a column. Let's pick up there. Would you please describe what, if anything, you did with respect to that other group of people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: This other group of people stayed there for about half an hour. You could hear planes. NATO bombing was expected, but the bombs exploded somewhere and the planes disappeared in the clouds in the sky.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, the witness, when mentioning a mixed group, he referred to civilians, able-bodied people, women, the elderly, et cetera. I would like the witness to clarify the meaning of able-bodied people. What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It means people of middle age.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What's the civilians? Are there civilians in their middle ages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you meant to mean by able-bodied people, soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] People of middle age, since I don't know who was a soldier and who wasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's proceed, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: This group, sir, that -- that you joined, can you describe for the Trial Chamber of what type of person that group consisted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: All categories were in that group, underaged, people of age, doctors, the rest of the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did it include both men and women, and, if so, in what proportion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: As for women, I could see a small number of women on the -- on the road. There were few women.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And at some point, was a decision made as to where this group you were with was going to go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: People were practically left to their own devices, to make their way to the free Tuzla territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Was that the objective of the group in which you found yourself, which you joined, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just for clarification, do you recall the date that this occurred?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: 11th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, would you tell the Trial Chamber why you decided to join that group rather than stay at your place of business or go with the other group towards Potocari?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: I decided -- well, it seemed based on my experience, up to then, it was unsafe. I felt it was unsafe, so I felt if I went to Potocari something bad would happen to me since I saw women, doctors, who had worked with me who had left through the woods to leave. I was afraid to go to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, what was your -- when you refer to feeling unsafe, what was it that you were feeling unsafe about that made you decide to join this group that was heading towards Tuzla rather than going to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: I was afraid that there would be separation of men and that men would be separated, abused, and finally killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did this group that you were with in fact set off towards Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: In what kind of formation were you organised?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: I would first describe it as a long, large column that was a couple of kilometres long, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And were you travelling on foot, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: How long did you walk that first day, 11 July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: On the 11th of July, in the evening, we were at the crossing. We were actually crossing the very first Serb lines at Buljim.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see that we're approaching the break. We're about to move into a fairly substantial area, and I would suggest this is a good time to take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We had a redaction, so we need a 30-minute break. Other -- is there anyone in the public gallery or not? None.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So we can safely have the break now for 30 minutes, and the curtains need not be drawn down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I understand, Ms. Condon, you would like to address the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I refrained from making any submission this morning in terms of our position as to preparedness to cross-examination. However, after having listened to the topics that perhaps have been covered by my learned friend with this witness, he has gone into a considerable amount of detail, which no criticism to him, that's often the way evidence comes out, but a considerable amount of detail that is simply not contained in the proofing notes that we were provided with this morning. I don't want to delay matters in terms of moving the cross-examination along. However, certainly from our perspective and given where we're most affected by in terms of where we stand, I would certainly make the application that I would seek the Court's indulgence to postpone my cross-examination until tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll attend to that. Mr. Meek, the same?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. During the break I researched the EDS system, and we would find it's useful to delay the Nikolic defence cross-examination until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... we also received certain documents relating to the credibility of the witness which have been disclosed to us only early this morning, and we would like to review them again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. We've just had the break to review with our client the material that has very lately been disclosed to us, and it's our position also that to properly prepare for cross-examination we would require overnight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll try to accommodate you as much as we can. In the meantime, I think you can choose amongst yourselves who is going to go first, unless you have done that already. And in order not to lose time, I think, at least the first cross-examinations can proceed on matters that you were already prepared for and then -- and then, of course, the rest will be reserved and you can cross-examine. But if we have one hour, I mean, let's not waste one hour, and we try to make good use of it. All right? So I think that should be acceptable, because I suppose you were already prepared for -- for some kind of cross-examination in any case. Yes, Mr. Thayer. Do you wish to comment on this or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I think that's a fair and sensible approach.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's bring the witness in, please. Thank you. And I take it that, overall, the original assessment of 3.5 hours for cross-examination is going to be -- has to be revised, has to be revised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How much longer do you think you have?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I thought you were referring to the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, the cross-examination but also --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I have, I believe, about an hour, maybe an hour and a quarter. It's hard to judge, but given the way we proceeded so far, I think I can stick to my two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So please go ahead, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Witness, before the break, you had testified about arriving in the area of Buljim. Do you recall what other areas you passed through before you reached that area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: Jaglici and Susnjari.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And at some point that evening, that is the evening of 11 July, did your portion of the column rest?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: Yes, there was a short rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And was there a reason for taking that rest, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: Yes, to reconnoiter the Serb lines, to see whether it was safe to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you make any effort with respect to administering to any other members of the column?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: The intention was to join up with the rest of the column, but this did not take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: What did you learn had happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: We learned that Srebrenica had finally fallen.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And during this rest, sir, did you try to provide any aid to anybody in the column?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: Yes. During that first break, nobody needed assistance since we were still in the territory that was in front of the Serb lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Where did you spend the night of 11 July, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: The early morning hours of the 11th of July was the time when we crossed the first Serb lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just for clarification, sir, I asked you where did you spend the night of 11 July, and your answer was the early morning hours of the 11th of July.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: We spent the night crossing those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you know where you found yourself in the morning of 12 July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: I don't know the precise location. I can just describe the terrain. We were in a valley surrounded by forests.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what, if anything, happened at that time, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: We took another rest, and we waited for the rest of the column, for the end part of the column, and then we would continue, all of us together.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you receive any information about the end part of the column?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: After a certain while we received information that the end part of the column had been cut off, that it came under heavy shelling, and that there were a lot of wounded in that end part of the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And at that point, did you make an attempt to aid the wounded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: An order was received for the medical personnel to go back and to tend to the dead and wounded. However, as we went back some 500 metres or so, we could not proceed all the way to the dead and wounded because of the heavy shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you return to that more forward portion of the column, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Of course I went back to the front part of the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you become aware at some point, during that day on 12 July, of the presence of Serb soldiers in your area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: Well, not far from us we could hear bullhorns calling out to all the Muslims in the forests to surrender and an ultimatum of sorts had been issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: When you say ultimatum of sorts, can you be more clear, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: A time line was set up. Three, five, or six hours was given to all of us to surrender, and if we did that, we would be transported safely to the free territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: From the position you were in, sir, the physical location, were you able to hear anything else significant?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: I could hear some APCs.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Could you hear upon what type of surface those APCs were driving, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: It was a hard surface, either asphalt or something of the kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you do anything in response to the ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: It was decided not to respond to the ultimatum and to continue moving towards the free territory at dusk.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Why did you decide not to surrender, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: I have already answered the question when I said why I didn't decide to go to Potocari. At that moment, I decided not to surrender because I expected something terrible would happen if I did. I felt safer in the woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: What, if anything, happened during that evening of 12 July, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: As night fell on the 12th of July, the first part of the column tried to cross an asphalt road, but at that moment, it seemed to me that a huge tree fell, and after that shelling started from all sides. We came under heavy artillery fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So where did you spend the night of 12 July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: I spent the night in the forest, by the streams, and I can't give you the exact location, as I'm not very familiar with the area anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what you did on 13 July, what you experienced?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: On the 13th of July we tried to cross an asphalt road, but this failed. We came across the first bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: On 13 July, did you become aware of the presence of Serb soldiers again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: Yes. As we were trying to cross that asphalt road, which apparently should have been crossed, we were discovered and APCs opened fire on the forest and the place where we were. That's why we returned to our original place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, sorry to interrupt, but if you go back up a couple of pages, it's page 38, line 20, to the question of yours asking whether he made an attempt to aid the wounded. He answered: "An order was received for the medical personnel to go back to tend to the dead and wounded." Could you clarify with the witness who ordered whom, on what capacity? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Witness, did you understand His Honour's question?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: From the top, from the head of the column, that was the information received. I suppose that this is the military leadership. I wouldn't know exactly. In any case, we were told to go back because information was received that the back of the column had been cut off and that there were a lot of dead and wounded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'll leave it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just one follow-up to Your Honour's question.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware of how that information was transmitted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Witness, turning your attention back to 13 July, did -- did you hear Serb soldiers on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: Again bullhorns were used, and they were calling upon all the Muslims who were in the forests carrying arms, not carrying arms, and it was said that they should have no fear, that they should surrender, and that they would all be transported to the free territory. If they didn't do that by a certain deadline, which was within three or four hours, then the Serb soldiers would start scouring the grounds and whoever was found there would be killed on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you, in fact, see anyone surrender, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: As I was hiding in a bush, I saw a lot of people heading towards the place from which they could hear the sound of the bullhorn.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you estimate how many people you saw surrendering at that time, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: I can't be sure. I can give you my estimate and say that the group consisted of some 50 men or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So how did you spend the evening of 13 July, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: On the 13th of July, we returned, and again there was an asphalt road that had to be crossed. Again we came across bodies. It was dark, and we couldn't see exactly who the bodies were and how people had been killed. We were not intimidated by that. We proceeded, and we managed to cross that asphalt road that we were supposed to cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That brings us to 14 July, sir. Can you describe what occurred that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: On that day we stayed in the forest, and we used the time to reconnoiter. When the night came, we then tried to cross those corridors as we had to cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what did you do next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: Again we managed to cross an asphalt road. We managed to cross a river as well. That river was rather deep. And we managed to get to a rather high elevation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what did you do after you reached that elevation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: As we reached that elevation, we stayed there and spent a whole night there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And at this point, sir, do you recall what the date was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: I must admit that I really don't remember. It was 12 years ago. It's very difficult for me to remember all those things precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, then I won't hold you to any particular dates for the next set of questions. Can you describe for the Trial Chamber what you did after you spent that day at the elevation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: In the early morning hours, we descended and reached a place called Glode, and we proceeded towards Bodjansko Brdo and Kamenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what did you do next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: There, in that sector, we stayed for a couple of days or three days trying to find food, picking mushrooms and other stuff.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall locating a particular burned house that belonged to someone in your group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: Yes. As soon as we crossed the river, a man in our group hailed from that area, we passed by his house. We found some burnt pots and pans that we used to prepare some food in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you know the name of this man, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall the name of this village in which you found this house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: Yes. The name of that village is Slano.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, at this point in your journey, sir, can you describe who else was with you in this group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: There were a few of my neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Could you name them, if you recall, for the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please use your judgement and tell us whether you need to go through this in private session or not. I mean, we are --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Depends on what you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: At this point, Your Honour, we can stay in open session. There will be questions recurring that will need private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go like that then.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall the names of these individuals, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what were their names?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: Should I give you all of their names?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If you would. If you can remember the names of the people in your group at that time. Just their names, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: I can't remember one name, but I do remember the rest. Ramiz Hrnjic, Salko Hrnjic, Muhamed Begic, Husein Hrnjic, Muhamed Mehmedovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: What did you do after you spent this time in this village of Slano?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: We continued towards the Otisce elevation, as I've already told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: After that, we descended into Glode, and then we proceeded towards Bodjansko Brdo, and then I went down to my place of birth.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, we'll need to move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: When you reached the area of Snagovo, do you recall approximately what day it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: It was approximately the 20th of July, in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I understand you don't have the dates at the top of your memory, but how is it that you estimate that it was approximately the 20th of July, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: Since I would be arrested shortly by the Serb forces, based on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you have an idea of how many days you had spent in the woods at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: Yes, we did have an idea. I spent 11 days in the woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You've described reaching the area of Snagovo. Do you recall, approximately, how much time you spent in that area of Snagovo before being arrested?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: We spent the night there, and then the next day until noon or the afternoon, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Would you please describe for the Trial Chamber what occurred the day that you were captured.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: The group of people that was with me included a man who was seriously ill. It was a man who had an ulcer, so he had strong pains. We tried to make tea from some herbs that we picked. We lit a fire in the woods, and we made the tea in order to ease his pain.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And at some point during that morning, did one of your group leave the group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: Yes. In the morning a person of our group left, actually in the course of the day, to reconnoiter the terrain and to see how we could proceed towards the free territory during the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall who that was, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It was Husein Hrnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And was Mr. Hrnjic armed at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you ever see or hear from Mr. Hrnjic again after that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: No. I didn't have the opportunity for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we may move into private session for one question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So after preparing or trying to prepare the tea for the man in pain, what happened next, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: At one point Serb soldiers appeared armed with rifles, and right away they ordered us to put our hands up. They surrounded us. After that, we put our hands behind our backs. They tied us, and then in a column we went.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, let me just interrupt you right there. The group that was captured with you, were these the same individuals whom you described to the Trial Chamber before, minus Mr. Husein Hrnjic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: Yes, the same people.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, if we may move into private session for just a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Back to your capture, Witness. You testified that you had placed your hands up, and I believe that you were -- had your hands tied behind your back. What happened next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: We went some 200 metres further from the place where we were arrested. We were thrown on the ground. We were lying on our chest. They started to hit us. They started to beat us with rifle butts and kicked us with their boots.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did other Serb soldiers arrive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: Yes. A few of them were there, and more kept coming in this place where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: How would you describe the scene at that point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: What can I say? You can imagine. It was horrible.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Was one of your companions able to escape?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: No -- yes. Yes. At the moment of arrest, one of the people from the group managed to throw himself into a nearby bush.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how were the events unfolding at this time, sir, as you recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: First there was the beating, then after that, insults. We were searched to see what we had on us. There was moaning, blood pouring out of noses, crying.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did your companions have any documents or belongings with them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: I think that some of them did have their IDs.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you have any identification or belongings with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: No, I didn't have anything at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did any of your other companions have a weapon at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Who had the weapon and what kind of weapon was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: Ramiz Hrnjic had an automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what became of that automatic rifle during the course of your capture, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall whether any of the Serb soldiers found it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: I don't know. He was arrested with the rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: When you say he was arrested with the rifle, was it in his hands or was it nearby him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: He had the rifle in his hand. Actually, on his shoulder.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, can you describe how quickly these events were taking place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: The beating, the abuse, insults lasted for about 20 minutes to half an hour. After that, I was lifted from the ground, and since I had no ID, they asked for my particulars, who I am, when I was born, where I was born, where I come from.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what did you tell them? Before you answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think at this point there's going to be a series of questions in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session. All right. Okay. Let's go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Witness, without referring to any particular names, you had testified that the other people captured with you were taken off at a particular distance from where you were. What happened next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: They weren't taken away. I left that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And then what do you recall happening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: We perhaps went from that place to an elevation some 2 to 300 metres away, and then I heard a burst of gunfire and then individual shots, and I panicked a lot. I began to tremble and shake.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Was the soldier you mentioned previously with you at the time and, if so, please don't mention his name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: What, if anything, did that soldier do when he saw your reaction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: He tried to console me, to get me to calm down. He said that they would try to do something for me and that I should try to survive, that it was a good thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did that soldier give you any food?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: Yes. He didn't, but others suggested that I should be given some food and water, if possible, since I didn't eat bread for 11 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: How long did you spend with these soldiers, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: We were together for two days and two nights.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: On the first night, were you restrained in any way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: Yes, I was. Since we were supposed to spend the night there, an order came that I should stay there with them also, but my hands were tied to a burned-out stove that was just lying there next to the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how about the second night? Were you restrained that night as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: I wasn't tied the second night.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And where did you physically sleep during that second night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: We were there on some mattresses where the other soldiers were sleeping also. So I was among them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: From spending this time among these soldiers, did you learn what their assignment was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did any of them tell you what they had been doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: At some point during those two days, did you see a vehicle arrive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: Yes, I did, the first evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you describe anything that you recall about that vehicle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: All I remember - I mean, I couldn't really see that much - was that it was a police vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you tell the Trial Chamber what happened next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: I didn't know what was happening. A group of soldiers rushed to this vehicle and stopped it from coming towards us. There was some sort of a barrier, and then there was a discussion, and after some 10 minutes or so, the vehicle went back the way it came.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: From what you could see, Witness, how would you characterise or describe that discussion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: It was very loud.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did it sound to you like a friendly discussion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you learn from the soldiers, who had been with you those two days, what this unfriendly discussion had been about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: What did they tell you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: They said that it was the police from Zvornik that had received information that there was a boy who was arrested and that they had him,

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: (redacted). But this crew that had arrested me opposed that, and they made them go back where they came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did any of the soldiers who had been with you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Let's go into private session for a short while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session now, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and thank you for those redactions.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, did any of the soldiers who had been guarding you tell you what the individuals who had arrived in the police vehicle told them would have happened to you had you been taken away?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: Yes. They told me that they had -- if -- that they handed me over to them, they would have skinned me alive. And these are the precise words that they used.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you eventually leave this Snagovo area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: Actually, it was at Zlatne Vode above Zvornik that we spent two days and two nights.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And at what time -- or could you describe how you left that area, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: Two buses came and all the soldiers and equipment that came with them was loaded onto those buses, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Witness, did the soldier tell you why the people from Zvornik would have skinned you alive? Did you hear the reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think we may need a redaction at line 8 of this page. I've been trying to avoid references to that particular location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take -- I take what you said, and let's redact the last -- after "buses," all the words after "buses" in line 8 on page 56, please. Thank you for pointing that out, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, if we may go into private session at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By all means. By all means. Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, while you were in Batkovici did you see anyone you knew or recognised from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: Yes. There were a few men whom I recognised, and there were some wounded men among them as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And without going into specifics, where did you recognise those wounded men from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: I first saw them in the hospital in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I think we have some problem with -- with the interpretation. What I heard from the witness -- he said that there were a lot of men whom I -- whom I recognised in Batkovici, and here I see on page 59, line 11, it says, "There were a few men." It changes the sense of what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he's been able to follow what has just been stated by Mr. Lazarevic. So, Witness, what's your comment on that? Did you see a few, or did you see quite a good number of persons you recognised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite a few.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I thank you, too, Mr. Lazarevic. Mr. Thayer, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: How long were you in the camp, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-106
utterances.text: Five months.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, with respect to the civilians with whom you were walking in the column, were there some whom you have never seen or heard from again since that time?
